title: Morning Edition
notes: It prioritizes developments since Friday’s morning edition: the FAA’s nationwide ground stop and the travel disruption that followed, reports that the U.S. has lost its measles-elimination status, the planned Trump–Xi–Putin meeting in Shenzhen, Zelensky’s account of a U.S. idea linking NATO membership to the Donbas, and the New Orleans river collision.
Ongoing stories — the Stellantis Brampton dispute, the Nvidia spy scandal, the Ukraine talks and Pope Leo’s Latin America tour — carry their original and updated dates.

Items described as planned, scheduled or reported — including the Trump–Xi–Putin meeting, the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame ceremony, Saturday’s WTA Finals semifinals, Clockenflap and the measles decision, which rests on unnamed sources — are not presented as completed or officially confirmed.

This edition has photos on the lead and on 21 of 24 other stories, using only Wikimedia Commons or U.S. government public-domain files, each credited and labelled as a file photo. None shows the events described.
Stories by region: U.S. 5, Canada 5, Hong Kong 5, China 5, World 5. Because it is a Saturday, several items are Friday news that broke after the previous edition.
provenance: Stories are compiled from the linked sources; labels describe the type of claim each story rests on.
Source pages were opened during this morning’s research between about 6:19 and 6:32 AM ET; each check time is the logged time that page was fetched.

China Daily is labelled State media; Sixth Tone is published by a state-owned Shanghai media group; RTHK is Hong Kong’s public broadcaster, and news.gov.hk and info.gov.hk are Hong Kong government sites.

Some pages (including Axios, the Washington Post, the South China Morning Post and a Reuters republication on Investing.com) returned access errors to automated fetches; those are access limits, not evidence that the reporting is wrong. Axios was read through a web reader; the others are not cited.
Where outlets gave different figures — the length of the ground stop and the number of people aboard the American Heritage — the edition states both.

stories.headline: FAA lifts a rare nationwide ground stop after more than four hours, but flight delays and cancellations roll into the weekend
stories.deck: The Federal Aviation Administration halted departures across the U.S. on Friday afternoon after what officials called a telecommunications failure, then reopened the airspace at 8:15 p.m. ET. Airlines were still working through thousands of delays and cancellations on Saturday.
stories.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration halted departures across the U.S. on Friday afternoon after what officials called a telecommunications failure, then reopened the airspace at 8:15 p.m. ET. Airlines were still working through thousands of delays and cancellations on Saturday. The FAA announced the stop at 3:54 p.m. ET “due to extraordinary circumstances,” and the BBC called it the longest nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks; FlightAware counted more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed an “incredibly old air traffic control system,” saying routers “got overloaded with data” and gave inconsistent readings, and warned the knock-on effects would last days. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyberattack — though, NPR noted, he could not rule one out entirely — and that the outage was not related to Thursday’s Microsoft outage. CBS News, citing multiple sources, said an update to the private network connecting the air traffic control system caused it to reboot. As of early Saturday FlightAware showed more than 6,200 delays and 3,400 cancellations, CNBC said; the SEC moved some college football games to Sunday, and NBA and NHL teams scrambled to travel. Air Canada also cancelled U.S.–Canada flights, and Hong Kong’s Airport Authority said four flights between the city and the U.S. were cancelled and 13 delayed, with delays expected until Sunday.
stories.why: Air travel across the country depends on decades-old equipment that can stop everything in an afternoon; the fight over who pays to modernize it will now be sharper — and anyone flying this weekend should check with their airline before heading out.
stories.label: Reported + official statement + unnamed sources
stories.note: The cause is the administration’s preliminary account; investigators were still working out exactly what failed. The report about a network update rests on unnamed sources cited by CBS News. Flight counts are FlightAware tallies at different times; outlets described the stop as lasting “more than four hours” (BBC) or “about five hours” (CBS).

stories.headline: U.S. has lost its measles-elimination status after 26 years, reports say, as two more deaths are reported
stories.deck: A Pan American Health Organization expert panel has concluded that measles has spread continuously in the United States for more than 12 months, ending the elimination status the country won in 2000, according to reports first published by The Wall Street Journal.
stories.summary: A Pan American Health Organization expert panel has concluded that measles has spread continuously in the United States for more than 12 months, ending the elimination status the country won in 2000, according to reports first published by The Wall Street Journal. Axios said the panel made the widely expected decision after a three-day meeting in Washington, and that the status hinges on whether the same strain keeps circulating for a year or more without a break. The CDC’s latest tally shows 5,412 confirmed cases so far in 2026, compared with 2,289 in all of 2025 — the most since 1991, Axios said. Al Jazeera reported that Pennsylvania and Wisconsin each announced another measles-associated death on Friday, including an infant in Wisconsin, bringing state-reported deaths this year to 10; the CDC’s own count is lower amid a dispute over how deaths are classified. Canada and the U.K. lost their elimination status in the past year. To regain it, the U.S. would need to go 12 months without continuous spread.
stories.why: The label is largely symbolic, but it confirms measles is again spreading on its own in pockets of low vaccination — including in New York — and keeping MMR shots up to date matters most for protecting babies too young to be vaccinated.
stories.label: Reported + unnamed sources
stories.note: The decision was reported citing people familiar with the matter; neither report Donna Daily read linked a published PAHO statement. Death counts differ between states and the CDC.

stories.headline: Tanker slams into a docked river cruise boat in New Orleans; everyone aboard survives and 32 are taken to hospital
stories.deck: A tanker that apparently lost its steering struck the paddlewheel cruise boat American Heritage at a New Orleans dock on Friday, flipping it into the Mississippi River. Officials said everyone was accounted for and no one was critically hurt.
stories.summary: A tanker that apparently lost its steering struck the paddlewheel cruise boat American Heritage at a New Orleans dock on Friday, flipping it into the Mississippi River. Officials said everyone was accounted for and no one was critically hurt. The much larger tanker Atlantic Asphalt hit the boat at about 12:30 p.m. local time, roughly two hours after it had docked for passengers to disembark at the end of an eight-day river cruise, CBS News and CBC News reported. Mayor Helena Moreno called it “a miracle on the Mississippi”: 32 people were taken to hospitals, none with critical injuries, and two harbor police officers were also hospitalized in good condition. Tugboat crews, port workers and police pulled dozens of people from the water as the boat listed and toppled. The U.S. Coast Guard said investigators were working to determine why the tanker lost control and that it was working to reopen the river, which it had closed after the collision.
stories.why: Nobody died, thanks largely to people nearby who rushed to help, but a ship losing control on one of America’s busiest rivers will raise hard questions about steering failures and safety near docked passenger boats.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: The cause had not been determined; “loss of steering” was the Coast Guard’s early assessment. Counts differ by source: the mayor said 180 people were aboard; Port NOLA, via CBS, said about 129 passengers plus crew.

stories.headline: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins Alaska’s governor race, the state’s first Democrat elected governor since 1998
stories.deck: Former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, won the race for Alaska governor after more than a week of counting, according to an Associated Press race call, beating three Republicans including one backed by President Trump.
stories.summary: Former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, won the race for Alaska governor after more than a week of counting, according to an Associated Press race call, beating three Republicans including one backed by President Trump. He will be the youngest governor in state history and replaces term-limited Republican Mike Dunleavy, NPR reported. Kreiss-Tomkins, from Sitka and known as JKT, campaigned as a “man of the middle,” promised a cabinet of Democrats, Republicans and independents, and was endorsed by Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski and three former governors. CBS News said he focused on affordability, full school funding and making oil and gas producers pay corporate income tax, and sought a moratorium on new data centers until lawmakers regulate them; his win means Democrats will hold 30 governorships. Voters also rejected a ballot measure to repeal Alaska’s open primaries and ranked-choice voting, keeping the system in place, according to another AP call.
stories.why: A Democrat winning statewide in Alaska — under a ranked-choice system voters just chose to keep — shows how broad this month’s midterm swing was, and makes the state a test of whether a bipartisan pitch can govern.

stories.headline: Rock & Roll Hall of Fame set to induct Wu-Tang Clan, Billy Idol and others in Los Angeles on Saturday, with Oasis, Sade and Iron Maiden staying away
stories.deck: The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame is set to induct its 2026 class at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles on Saturday night, but several big-name inductees are skipping the ceremony, the Associated Press reported.
stories.summary: The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame is set to induct its 2026 class at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles on Saturday night, but several big-name inductees are skipping the ceremony, the Associated Press reported. The class includes Billy Idol, Phil Collins, Sade, Queen Latifah, New Order with Joy Division, Luther Vandross, Iron Maiden, Oasis and Wu-Tang Clan. Oasis will not attend — Liam Gallagher posted that it was “too far to be going for the night” — Iron Maiden is touring Australia and Sade is sitting it out; Collins is expected but will not play for health reasons. Wu-Tang Clan, Queen Latifah and MC Lyte are expected to appear and probably perform, and Idol will take the stage with guitarist Steve Stevens. Fela Kuti will become the first African-born artist in the hall and Celia Cruz the first member who sang primarily in Spanish. Unlike recent years, the show will not stream live; an edited version airs on ABC and Disney+ on Dec. 9.
stories.why: Hip-hop could steal the night: Wu-Tang Clan, plus Queen Latifah and MC Lyte, headline a class that also marks firsts for African and Spanish-language music — even with several rock stars staying home.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: The ceremony had not taken place when this edition was compiled; performers and appearances can change.

stories.headline: Canada and the Philippines conclude free-trade talks in Manila, with signing expected in 2027
stories.deck: Prime Minister Mark Carney and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. oversaw the signing of a document formally ending negotiations for a Philippines-Canada free-trade agreement, which is expected to be signed next year.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. oversaw the signing of a document formally ending negotiations for a Philippines-Canada free-trade agreement, which is expected to be signed next year. The talks began just over a year ago after Carney rebooted an idea Ottawa first explored in 2015, CBC News reported. During consultations, businesses broadly supported the deal while civil-society groups raised concerns about the Philippines’ record on the environment, labour and human rights. Carney is in Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit, and Canada is also pursuing a broader trade deal with the ASEAN bloc. “A ship that stays in the harbour is safe, but that’s not what a ship is for,” Carney told Marcos, according to Global News.
stories.why: With U.S. trade talks still unresolved, each new deal in Asia is part of Ottawa’s push to sell more beyond its biggest customer.

stories.note: Concluding negotiations is not the same as signing or ratifying; the deal’s text had not been published.

stories.headline: Carney says Canada won’t sign a U.S. trade deal without a viable auto sector, as Ottawa and Ontario pitch Stellantis to keep Brampton open
stories.deck: Prime Minister Mark Carney said in Manila on Saturday that Canada will not settle for a U.S. trade deal that is not consistent with a viable Canadian auto sector, a day after Ottawa and Ontario said they had put an “aggressive package” to Stellantis to stop the sale of its Brampton plant.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said in Manila on Saturday that Canada will not settle for a U.S. trade deal that is not consistent with a viable Canadian auto sector, a day after Ottawa and Ontario said they had put an “aggressive package” to Stellantis to stop the sale of its Brampton plant. Carney called autos “one of the most challenging issues” in the talks but said progress was being made, and revealed a “long, substantive conversation” with President Trump this week with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and chief of staff Stephen Miller on the line, The Canadian Press reported. He also said Ottawa was “not satisfied in any way” with Stellantis’s partial approach and expects it to respect its commitments to workers. On Friday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the governments were “still in solution mode to prevent the sale” of the Brampton assembly plant to defence contractor Roshel, and that she, Unifor and Ontario’s Vic Fedeli would meet Stellantis global CEO Antonio Filosa to pitch scenarios to keep the plant “warm” until new products return, CBC News reported.
stories.why: Autos are where Canada’s U.S. trade fight hits workers hardest, and Brampton is the test of whether Ottawa can make a company that took public money keep its promises.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: The details of the governments’ package were not made public. Continues coverage from the Nov 12 editions.

stories.headline: B.C. arbitrator imposes what the union calls the first contract for Amazon workers in North America; Amazon calls it unfair
stories.deck: About 800 Amazon workers in Delta, B.C., are now covered by what their union, Unifor, says is the first binding collective agreement for the company’s workers in North America, after an independent arbitrator imposed a three-year deal on Friday.
stories.summary: About 800 Amazon workers in Delta, B.C., are now covered by what their union, Unifor, says is the first binding collective agreement for the company’s workers in North America, after an independent arbitrator imposed a three-year deal on Friday. Unifor says the contract raises hourly pay to $29 by its end, improves severance protection and adds a week of vacation for workers with 10 years of service. B.C.’s Labour Relations Board ruled in August that the dispute should be settled by binding arbitration, over Amazon’s objections. Amazon vice-president J. Ofori Agboka said the process was “improper, unfair and defies common sense,” that workers were not allowed to vote on the deal and that union dues could leave some taking home less, adding that the company would go to court if necessary, CBC News reported.
stories.why: Amazon has fought unions across North America, so a contract imposed in B.C. is a precedent labour groups elsewhere will cite — and one the company says it may challenge in court.
stories.label: Reported + official statement + claim
stories.note: Contract terms are as described by Unifor; Amazon disputes the process.

stories.summary: Canadian electronic duo Bob Moses say their 2021 collaboration with British musician Elderbrook, “Inner Light,” has picked up more than 50 million extra streams since it featured in an extended Grand Theft Auto VI trailer in late August. stories.summary: Hong Kong’s economy grew 5.2% year on year in the third quarter, the government said on Friday, as it raised its full-year growth forecast to 4.8% from a range of 3.5% to 4.5%. Fan said the economy was “poised for a strong full-year performance” but that geopolitical tensions, U.S. monetary policy and trade protectionism warranted close monitoring.

stories.headline: Hong Kong plans stricter checks on proxy votes at flat owners’ meetings instead of a cap, home affairs chief says
stories.deck: Hong Kong will require both flat owners and their proxies to sign declarations and leave contact details, rather than capping how many proxy votes one person can hold, Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak said on Saturday.
stories.summary: Hong Kong will require both flat owners and their proxies to sign declarations and leave contact details, rather than capping how many proxy votes one person can hold, Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak said on Saturday. Speaking on an RTHK radio programme, Mak said a month-long consultation on changes to the Building Management Ordinance drew 550 written submissions, which broadly backed clearer thresholds for major maintenance works and stronger proxy rules. About half opposed a numerical cap on proxies as hard to enforce once forms are sealed and opened together. Under the plan, owners would declare they know about the meeting and agenda, and representatives would declare that the person authorising them is the genuine owner. “Verification is more effective than a prescribed cap,” Mak said.
stories.why: Owners’ corporation votes decide costly repair contracts, so how proxy votes are checked affects what many families end up paying for building works.

stories.note: These are proposals following consultation; they still need to go through legislation.
